title: Plans: what's coming up
title_target: ແຜນການຂ້າງໜ້າ — Phěen-kaan khàang-nâa
goal: Talk about tomorrow and next month: plans, intentions, hopes, and conditions — plus how to say something isn't certain yet without promising too much.

dialogs.title: ບົດສົນທະນາ — Planning next month
dialogs.intro: Budi and Bounmy talk about plans. Notice how many sentences are deliberately left uncertain — in Laos, promising something too firmly is actually seen as unwise.

notes: **ຊິ si is the future marker Lao people use every day.** *ຊິໄປ* (will go), *ຊິກິນ* (will eat). Its twin *ຈະ ja* is also correct, but sounds more formal and more Thai — in Lao conversation, *ຊິ* is far more common. ⚠️ If you learn from books published in Thailand, you'll see *ຈະ* everywhere; use *ຊິ* and you'll immediately sound more local.

**ຢາກ yàak = "want", ຕັ້ງໃຈ tâng-jai = "intend".** The first is a wish, the second a resolve. *ຢາກໄປ* (want to go), *ຕັ້ງໃຈຊິໄປ* (intend to go). Notice that *ຕັ້ງໃຈ* can be combined with *ຊິ*, while *ຢາກ* can't.
**ຄົງ khóng = "probably", ອາດ àat = "maybe".** *ຄົງ* is more certain than *ອາດ*. Both often pair with *ຊິ*: *ຄົງຊິໄປ* (will probably go), *ອາດຊິບໍ່ໄປ* (might not go).
**ຖ້າ… ຊິ… thàa… si… is the full conditional pattern.** *ຖ້າມີເວລາ ຂ້ອຍຊິໄປ* (if I have time, I'll go). The *ຖ້າ* clause comes first, and no other link word is needed in between.
**ຫວັງວ່າ wǎng vàa = "hope that".** *ຂ້ອຍຫວັງວ່າ…* opens a hope. Remember *ວ່າ vàa* from unit 13, which introduces reported speech; here it's used again with a different verb.

**ແນ່ນອນ nèe-nawn = "definitely, certainly".** *ໄດ້ແນ່ນອນ* (definitely can), *ແນ່ນອນບໍ່* (are you sure?). For things that aren't certain, Lao people prefer *ຄົງ* — and that isn't doubt but courtesy: not promising more than you can keep.
**ດົນປານໃດ dón paan dai = "how long".** The phrase *ປານໃດ paan dai* means "how (much)" and pairs with other adjectives: *ໄກປານໃດ* (how far), *ແພງປານໃດ* (how expensive).
**ຄ່ອງ khàwng = "fluent".** *ເວົ້າໄດ້ຄ່ອງ* (can speak fluently). You'll often hear it from people praising your progress — and what they usually mean isn't your grammar, but your courage.
**ບ້ານເກີດ bâan kòet = "hometown", literally "birth village".** Being invited to someone's *ບ້ານເກີດ* is a serious sign of friendship in Laos — far bigger than being invited to dinner in the city.

grammars.title: Degrees of certainty, from doubtful to sure
after: Notice that **the negative goes in different places** depending on what you mean. *ບໍ່ຊິໄປ* = "won't go" (rejecting the plan). *ອາດຊິບໍ່ໄປ* = "might not end up going" (unsure). A subtle difference, but people hear it.

blocks.text: Remember the pattern from unit 7: **ໜ້າ *nâa*** for what's coming, **ແລ້ວ *lèeo*** or **ກາຍ *kaai*** for what's past. With those two words you can build a time marker for any unit of time without memorizing each one.

rows: ມື້ອື່ນເຈົ້າຊິເຮັດຫຍັງ
ຂ້ອຍຕັ້ງໃຈຊິ…
ຍັງບໍ່ໄດ້ຕັດສິນໃຈ
ແລ້ວແຕ່ອາກາດ
ຖ້າວ່າງ ຂ້ອຍຊິມາ
ຂ້ອຍຊິບອກເຈົ້າພາຍຫຼັງ
ຫວັງວ່າຊິໄດ້ພົບກັນອີກ
*wǎng vàa si dâi phop kan ìik*

blocks.text: **ແລ້ວແຕ່… *lèeo tèe…*** means "it depends on…" — the twin of *ແລ້ວແຕ່ເຈົ້າ* (up to you) from unit 11. *ແລ້ວແຕ່ອາກາດ* (depends on the weather), *ແລ້ວແຕ່ວຽກ* (depends on work). It's an honest answer, used constantly for plans that aren't settled.

An important cultural note. In Laos, plans are often stated loosely on purpose, and a last-minute cancellation is not an insult. The *ບໍ່ເປັນຫຍັງ* (no problem) that follows a cancellation is almost always sincere. If you're used to strict schedules, this is the biggest adjustment you'll need to make — and the easiest way to adjust is to reconfirm on the day itself, without pressing.
